extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in probability theory / stochastic processes (Brownian motion and PDE connections)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of limit theorems for empirical processes, Brownian bridge, the law of the iterated logarithm, and probabilistic representations/solutions of PDEs (heat equation, inhomogeneous heat equation, Feynman–Kac, Dirichlet problem) via Brownian motion and martingales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donsker convergence and continuous functional mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Donsker’s theorem implies B_n(·) ⇒ B(·) (a Brownian motion), and if ψ(ω)=max_{0≤t≤1} |ω(t)−tω(1)| is continuous from C[0,1] to R then mapping B_n → ψ(B_n) and limits follow (Theorem 8.4.3: D_n ⇒ max_{0≤t≤1} |B_t − tB_1|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Donsker’s functional CLT and continuous-mapping theorem to pass from convergence of empirical process B_n to convergence of functionals like sup norms; account for negligible terms (e.g., Zn+1/n→1 a.s., Zn+1−Zn scaled →0 in probability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/identification of Brownian bridge
rubrics_metrics.description: The process {B_t − tB_1, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1} has the same distribution as {B_t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 | B_1 = 0}; this process is denoted B^0_t and called the Brownian bridge (equation (8.4.3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret conditioning on an event of probability 0 via the finite-dimensional conditional densities (see (8.4.4)); use this identification when deriving distributions for functionals of the bridge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-dimensional distributions of Brownian motion conditional on B1=0
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Gaussian transition densities p_t(x,y) = (2πt)^{−1/2} exp(−(y−x)^2/2t) to compute f.d.d.'s of the bridge; this provides the rigorous meaning of conditioning on B1=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covariance structure of Brownian bridge
rubrics_metrics.description: For s<t, E((B_s − sB_1)(B_t − tB_1)) = s(1 − t) (equation (8.4.5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this covariance (and mean 0) to characterise the bridge as a Gaussian process and to check equality in distribution with other representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional transition law of the Brownian bridge
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditional distribution (B^0_t | B^0_s = x) is Normal with mean x(1−t)/(1−s) and variance (1−t)(1−s)/(1−s) (see (8.4.7) and surrounding derivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the bivariate normal conditioning formula and the bridge covariance to derive transition densities and verify the Markov property for the bridge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection principle series for killed Brownian density (Theorem 8.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The density of B_t on the event {T_a ∧ T_b > t} is given by the infinite series (8.4.8): Σ_{n=−∞}^∞ [P_x(B_t = y + 2n(b−a)) − P_x(B_t = 2b − y + 2n(b−a))].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive exit/time-restricted densities by repeated reflections (ρ_a(y)=2a−y) and take limits; visualize the alternating ± terms as in Figure 8.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of maximum of Brownian bridge and Kolmogorov–Smirnov law
rubrics_metrics.description: P_0(max_{0≤t≤1} |B^0_t| < b) = Σ_{m=−∞}^∞ (−1)^m e^{−2 m^2 b^2} (equation (8.4.12)), which yields the limit distribution of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this infinite-series expression to compute tail probabilities for the supremum of the bridge; apply by transforming data via F(X_i) to test goodness-of-fit against F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal inequality for Brownian motion over [0,1] (8.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine reflection principle and Gaussian tail estimates to bound suprema probabilities; this identity is key in LIL proofs via Borel–Cantelli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaussian tail asymptotics (8.5.2–8.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these bounds to estimate probabilities like P_0(B_t > (t f(t))^{1/2}); combine with scaling to analyze rare events along sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of the iterated logarithm for Brownian motion (Theorem 8.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: limsup_{t→∞} B_t/(2 t log log t)^{1/2} = 1 almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove upper bound via Borel–Cantelli on exponentially spaced times and Gaussian tail asymptotics; get lower bound by constructing independent increments on those spacings and applying second Borel–Cantelli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hartman–Wintner LIL for random walks (Theorem 8.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_i are i.i.d. with E X_i = 0 and finite variance, then limsup_{n→∞} S_n/(2 n log log n)^{1/2} = 1 a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed the random walk into Brownian motion (Skorokhod representation) as S_n = B(T_n) with T_n/n → 1 a.s.; reduce to continuous LIL by controlling (S_[t] − B_t)/ (t log log t)^{1/2} → 0 (equation (8.5.7)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strassen invariance principle (Theorem 8.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under i.i.d. X_i with E X_i = 0 and finite variance, the limit set of scaled interpolated partial sums Z_n(·) = (2 n log log n)^{−1/2} S(n·) equals K = { f : f(x) = ∫_0^x g(y) dy with ∫_0^1 g(y)^2 dy ≤ 1 }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives functional (compact) description of all subsequential limits of normalized paths; contains the LIL as a projection and yields structural information about how large deviations occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale representation via Ito for C^2 functions (Theorem 9.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If v ∈ C^2 and E ∫_0^t |∇v(B_s)|^2 ds < ∞ for all t, then v(B_t) − (1/2) ∫_0^t Δv(B_s) ds is a continuous martingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Ito’s formula plus integrability of gradient to identify martingale part and finite-variation part; this is the basic tool linking harmonicity and martingales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected exit time from ball (Theorem 9.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For |x|<R, E_x S_R = (R^2 − |x|^2)/d (S_R the hitting time of sphere of radius R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply martingale |B_t|^2 − d t and optional stopping to compute mean exit times from balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental harmonic functions and optional stopping (ϕ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ϕ(x) = log|x| when d=2 and ϕ(x)=|x|^{2−d} when d≥3; in both cases Δϕ=0 and ϕ(x) = E_x ϕ(B_τ) for τ an exit time from annulus (Lemma 9.1.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these explicit harmonic functions to derive hitting probabilities and recurrence/transience results via optional stopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hitting probability formula in d=2 (9.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For d=2 and r<R, P_x(S_r < S_R) = (log R − log |x|)/(log R − log r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialize the ϕ-harmonic formula and pass to limits (e.g., R→∞) to deduce recurrence statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hitting probability formula in d≥3 (9.1.4 and 9.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formulas show transient behaviour in d≥3: nonunit probability to ever hit a fixed ball when starting outside it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence in dimension two and non-hitting of points in d≥2 (9.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: In d=2 Brownian motion is recurrent (visits any open set infinitely often). For d≥2, P_x(S_0 < ∞) = 0 for all x (Brownian motion will not hit 0 at a positive time even if it starts there).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use harmonic ϕ and limiting arguments; continuity and Markov property extend the non-hitting conclusion to x=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape to infinity in d≥3 (Theorems 9.1.4 and 9.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: As t→∞, |B_t|→∞ a.s. in d≥3 (Theorem 9.1.4). More precisely, for positive decreasing g(t), P_0(|B_t| ≤ g(t) i.o.) is 1 or 0 according as ∫_∞ g(t)^{d−2}/t dt diverges or converges (Dvoretsky–Erdős criterion, Theorem 9.1.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine stopping-time estimates, scaling relations, and integrability tests to determine rates at which Brownian motion escapes to infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale characterization for heat equation solutions (Theorem 9.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u satisfies ut = (1/2)Δu in (0,∞)×R^d and sufficient smoothness, then M_s = u(t−s, B_s) is a local martingale on [0,t].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Ito’s formula to space-time process (t−s,B_s); vanishing of the PDE terms gives martingale property—this is the probabilistic representation mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of bounded solution to heat equation (Theorem 9.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a bounded solution u of ut = (1/2)Δu with u(0,x)=f(x) (f bounded continuous), then u(t,x) ≡ E_x f(B_t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bounded martingale M_s = u(t−s,B_s), uniform integrability and martingale convergence to identify the solution as expectation of initial data under Brownian motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity of heat-kernel solution (Theorems 9.2.3–9.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If v(t,x)=E_x f(B_t) with f bounded continuous, then v ∈ C^{1,2}, satisfies ut=(1/2)Δu, and v(t,x)=∫ (2πt)^{−d/2} e^{−|x−y|^2/(2t)} f(y) dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify interchange of differentiation and integration using Gaussian kernel smoothness; this gives explicit smoothing and shows initial continuity at t→0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation for inhomogeneous heat equation (Theorems 9.3.1–9.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For ut = (1/2)Δu + g with initial f≡0, if u bounded on [0,T]×R^d then u(t,x)=E_x ∫_0^t g(B_s) ds, and M_s = u(t−s,B_s) + ∫_0^s g(B_r) dr is a local martingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similar Ito/optional-stopping arguments as homogeneous case; verify continuity at t→0 via dominated estimates when g bounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness under Hölder condition for inhomogeneous forcing (Theorem 9.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If g is Hölder continuous, then the solution v(t,x)=E_x ∫_0^t g(B_s) ds belongs to C^{1,2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address potential singular integrability near small times; Hölder continuity of g supplies the extra regularity to permit differentiation under the integral and control singularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feynman–Kac representation for potential term (Theorems 9.4.1–9.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For ut = (1/2)Δu + c(x)u with bounded continuous c and bounded continuous f, the bounded solution (if any) is v(t,x) = E_x[ f(B_t) exp(c_t) ] where c_t = ∫_0^t c(B_s) ds; moreover M_s = u(t−s,B_s) exp(c_s) is a local martingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive via generalized Ito formula with multiplicative functional exp(c_s); check boundedness/uniform integrability to obtain uniqueness and initial continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness under Hölder conditions for Feynman–Kac (Theorem 9.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and c are Hölder continuous (and bounded), then v(t,x)=E_x[f(B_t) exp(c_t)] ∈ C^{1,2} and so solves ut=(1/2)Δu + c u.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the homogeneous/inhomegeneous cases via integral decomposition (equation (9.4.3)); use local Hölder estimates to control convolution-like terms and obtain differentiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic solution to Dirichlet problem (Theorem 9.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bounded C^2 solution u exists of Δu=0 in open set G with continuous boundary values f, and if P_x(τ<∞)=1 for all x∈G, then u(x) = E_x f(B_τ) where τ = inf{t : B_t ∉ G}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use martingale M_t = u(B_{t∧τ}) and uniform integrability to pass to limit and recover boundary value; this gives the Poisson representation when boundary is regular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averaging property and smoothness of harmonic solutions (Theorems 9.5.3–9.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If v ∈ C^2 and harmonic in G then v(x) = E_x v(B_{τ_B}) for small balls B and hence v ∈ C^∞ via averaging properties (harmonic functions are infinitely differentiable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Taylor expansion, martingale properties of increments and spherical averaging to bootstrap smoothness to C^∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary regularity / definition of regular point
rubrics_metrics.description: A boundary point y ∈ ∂G is regular if P_y(τ = 0) = 1 (i.e., Brownian motion started at y exits immediately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularity controls whether probabilistic solution attains the boundary value at y; verify regularity via capacities, geometric conditions (cone condition) or local thickness of complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity at regular boundary points (Theorem 9.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If y is regular and x_n ∈ G with x_n → y then v(x_n) → f(y), where v(x)=E_x f(B_τ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower-semicontinuity of x→P_x(τ≤t) and small-time control of Brownian oscillation to show mass of exit distribution concentrates near y as starting points approach y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower semicontinuity of hitting probabilities (Lemma 9.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For t>0, x → P_x(τ ≤ t) is lower semicontinuous: if x_n→x then liminf_{n→∞} P_{x_n}(τ≤t) ≥ P_x(τ≤t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via Chapman-Kolmogorov decomposition: x→P_x(B_s ∈ G^c for some s∈(ε,t]) is continuous for each ε>0; let ε↓0 to obtain lower semicontinuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone condition for boundary regularity (Theorem 9.5.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists a cone V with vertex y and r>0 such that V∩D(y,r) ⊂ G^c, then y is regular (Py(τ=0)=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spherical-symmetry of Gaussian increments to show positive probability of entering complement arbitrarily quickly and Blumenthal's 0–1 law to conclude immediate exit holds a.s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exit distribution (Poisson kernel) for half-space (Theorem 9.5.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the half-space H = { (x,y): y>0 }, the Poisson kernel h_θ(x,y) = C_d y/(|x−θ|^2 + y^2)^{d/2} is harmonic in H and gives the exit density: u(x,y)=∫_{R^{d−1}} h_θ(x,y) f(θ,0) dθ solves the Dirichlet problem in H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalize C_d so that ∫ h_θ(0,1) dθ = 1; in d=2 this yields the Cauchy density for the horizontal coordinate at first hitting of the boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples: boundary condition may fail (punctured disc, Lebesgue’s thorn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show the probabilistic representation v(x)=E_x f(B_τ) need not attain the prescribed boundary values everywhere: e.g., punctured disc in d=3 (a line removed) or Lebesgue’s thorn in d≥3 where complement is too thin near a boundary point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to illustrate that geometric regularity (thickness, cone condition) matters; when complement is too small near a boundary point the exit distribution may avoid parts of the boundary and boundary values need not be attained.
